text: Every data format you'll touch starting in Chapter 3 — a JSON API response, a database row, a pipeline record — is naturally key-value shaped. A dictionary is Python's native way to represent exactly that: one record with named fields, instead of a list where you have to remember that index two happens to mean customer name.

Here's one order as a dictionary — order ID, customer name, region, quantity, price, status, all named. Compare this to Lesson 3's fields bracket two from a split line: order bracket customer_name is self-documenting. Anyone reading the code, including future you, knows exactly what's being accessed.

Dictionaries are mutable, so you can update an existing key, like changing status to Delivered, or add a brand new key, like a tracking number, any time after creation — the same way lists are mutable.

Accessing a key that doesn't exist with square brackets raises a KeyError and crashes your script — dangerous once you're processing real records where not every row has every field. dot get solves that: it returns None, or an explicit default you choose, instead of crashing. Use it any time a field might legitimately be missing.

This is the pattern everything from Chapter 4's pandas onward builds on: a list where each item is a dictionary representing one row. It's exactly the shape of a CSV file, just living in Python. A list of dicts, looped over, with a calculation per row, is the mental model for almost every pipeline you'll build.

You can now model a real record as a dictionary and a batch of records as a list of dictionaries. Next lesson: control flow — if, elif, else for branching, and for and while loops for processing every row in that batch, including the ones that need to be skipped.
